vo: The biggest companies of the next decade may not be built with big teams. They may be built by one person, leading a team of agents.
A business that once needed twenty people can now run on a founder, a couple of part-timers, and Bots handling the routine work.
In this series, we'll go through it in six moves. This first part is about the most important one: choosing what problem to solve.
Before you build anything, decide what you're building. And start with the problem, not the idea. Your idea may sound great. But what pain does it fix?
Think of a vitamin versus a painkiller. A vitamin is nice to have. A painkiller is something people need right now.
When you have a migraine, you'll pay almost anything for the pill. With no pain, even a cheap vitamin is a hard sell. The bigger the pain, the bigger the money.
Now let the Bot do the searching. Say you run a gym. Tell it your background, and ask for fifty specific, observable problems gym owners face right now.
Read the list and ask: are people already trying to pay to fix these? Keep the top three. Those become the problems your offer will solve.
Next, have the Bot write a short message about those three pains, and send it to ten people in that market. Not a pitch. Just a question.
Don't ask for the sale, ask for advice. Ask for the sale and you get advice. Ask for advice, and you get the sale.
On the call, they'll often ask what you're building. That's your moment. Present your offer, and invite them to be your first customer.
Already have a business? Then you know your customer. Run the same search anyway, to sharpen your message around the pain you solve.
Now you're solving the right problem, and customers start to arrive. But your time piles up fast. Calls, delivery, everything lands on you. That's when you need agents.
Most people automate the wrong thing first, and end up busier without earning more. The right problem in the wrong order costs money. So next, we climb in order.
